title: Indonesia captures the blacklisted MV NIKA on 12 July 2019 after INTERPOL tracking supported by OceanMind and Global Fishing Watch; the sources describe analyst tracking, not an AI detection
summary: MV NIKA seized by Indonesia 12 Jul 2019 after INTERPOL tracking with OceanMind and GFW; captain convicted, owner fined, vessel forfeited; no fetched source documents an AI detection.
account: INTERPOL reported on 22 July 2019 that the MV NIKA, a vessel suspected of illegal fishing in the Southern Ocean and owned by the same company as the blacklisted STS 50 intercepted in Indonesia in 2018, had been detained by Indonesian authorities. INTERPOL tracked the vessel's movement with support from the UK not-for-profit OceanMind, sending daily reports to Indonesia, New Zealand, Panama, the UK and the US, and hourly updates aided by Global Fishing Watch (GFW) as it approached Indonesian waters. GFW's own account (23 July 2019) says the vessel had been tracked since February 2019 with the help of GFW analyst Imam Prakoso after it illegally switched off its tracking system, that a live multi-way communication between Indonesian naval and fishery officials, INTERPOL and GFW analyst Charles Kilgour exchanged information, that GFW analysts helped predict its course and identify rendezvous points, and that Indonesian patrol boats ORCA 2 and ORCA 3 intercepted it on 12 July 2019 at 08:06 local time. The earlier verifier's reason records, from a UK Government Blue Belt blog of 5 June 2021 that could not be re-fetched (bluebelt.blog.gov.uk returned 404 on 20 October 2026), that the Indonesian Supreme Court gave its verdict on 27 February 2020, the captain was convicted, the owner fined Rp300,000,000 and the vessel forfeited. None of the fetched sources describes a machine-learning or AI detection; OceanMind's homepage says only, in general terms, that it uses satellites, AI and human expertise.
purpose: Vessel tracking and analysis to support fisheries enforcement against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing; the capture was the intended use, but the sources attribute it to analysts and inter-agency coordination rather than to an AI output.
system: Global Fishing Watch vessel-tracking platform and analysts; OceanMind analysis for INTERPOL (no AI component documented for this case)
deployer: INTERPOL Global Fisheries Enforcement programme; Indonesian naval and fisheries authorities (patrol boats ORCA 2 and ORCA 3)
domain: Fisheries enforcement / illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing
segment: International police cooperation and national maritime enforcement
taxonomy_note: Loose fit: the benefit is an enforcement action against a blacklisted IUU vessel. The AI role is undocumented: INTERPOL and GFW describe analyst tracking of AIS data and predicted rendezvous points, and OceanMind's method is not described; the court outcome is carried from the earlier verifier's reason because the Blue Belt blog could not be re-fetched.

ratings.reason: No individual beneficiary is identified in any fetched source.
Unassessed: Indonesian authorities and INTERPOL obtained a capture, a conviction and a forfeiture, but no fetched source attributes any part of the result to an AI output, so no depth is assigned.
Unassessed: one blacklisted vessel removed from Southern Ocean fishing; the contribution of any AI system is undocumented and the deterrent effect is not quantified.

ai_role.statement: No fetched source documents an AI or machine-learning role. INTERPOL's release says it tracked the vessel with support from OceanMind and that hourly updates were aided by contributions from Global Fishing Watch; GFW's own article credits named analysts who tracked AIS data, predicted the course and identified rendezvous points, and does not mention algorithms, machine learning or automated detection; OceanMind's homepage states only that it uses satellites, AI and human expertise in general. The AI role is therefore undocumented rather than established, and the record rests on INTERPOL's release, GFW's own account and the earlier verifier's reading of the Blue Belt blog. The court outcome (Supreme Court verdict of 27 February 2020, conviction, Rp300,000,000 fine, forfeiture) is carried from the earlier verifier's reason, which read a UK Government Blue Belt blog post of 5 June 2021 that no longer resolves and has no archived copy.
